           Thus it seems that in Nigeria, more than in some of the
       other countries of the world, there is a need to study the situa­
       tion of that particular discipline which helps people to focus
       attention on the interaction between law and society. This is
       necessary because a profound understanding of this situation
       can eventually lead to the development of a proper Nigerian le­
       gal system.
           This paper, therefore, intends to engage in an analysis of
       the situation of the sociology of law in Nigeria. Some of the
       pertinent questions we intend to find answers to are (1) Curren­
       cy of the discipline in this society; (2) The interest generated
       in the people, particularly scholars, in this discipline; (3) Inhi­
       bitions to the generation of interest in the discipline; (4) The
       possibilities of generating such interest etc. It is believed that
       the answers provided to these questions should assist not only in
       enhancing the development of sociology of law as a discipline,
       but it should lead to the enhancement of the public’s awareness
       about the interaction between law and society and thus influ­
       ence the quality and performance of the Nigerian legal system.
       This study should also provide some information on the situa­
       tion of sociology of law in Nigeria to interested scholars in oth­
       er countries of the world.


       1.   Methodology.

           The study is intended to cover the whole of Nigeria. The
       specific areas of study are the Sociology Departments and Fac­
       ulties of Law in the Universities in Nigeria.

     Economics was one of those disciplines. In the 1800s, sev­
eral leading professors in the law faculty were responsible for a
combination of subjects consisting of law, so-called «state
economics», and statistics, «state economics» and statistics
became the subjects of a separate chair in 1886, and a two
year course « state economics » was introduced as early as in
1905. But also economics in a more modem sense was first de­
veloped within the context of the law faculty. Norwegian
academia saw the planning and first development of economics
in the modern sense in the 1930s, after the world wide eco­
nomic crisis beginning in 1929, in which Norway was also in­
volved. To a large extent, the subject was developed as a re­
sponse to that crisis, a crisis which legal dogmatics and law
proper was not fit to handle, and a full fledged major in eco­
nomics was introduced by law in 1934 — in a division within
the law faculty. The candidates with degrees in economics
largely came after World War II, in the late 1940s and the
1950s. The subject of economics, and the major in that sub­
ject, remained in the law faculty until 1963, when it became a
part of the social science faculty which was established that
year. In terms of content, the economics which was taught in
the law faculty was strongly inspired by Keynesian economic
thinking. The whole first generation of Norwegian economists,
who manned top positions in the Norwegian social democratic
political system and state bureaucracy after World War II,
were thus educated within the general context of the law facul­
ty-
     Sociology was another of the disciplines which received its
first development within the context of the law faculty. But un­
like economics, sociology was not introduced as a separate
major subject. Rather, it became an integrated part of the
teaching of law. General sociology became an obligatory sub­
ject for law students during the first and introductory part of
their study as early as in 1936 — long before sociology as such

Thomas Mathiesen                              607


was developed at the University of Oslo. In principle, the law
students were to be given a broad introduction to social scien­
tific thinking through the subject. After World War II, in the
late 1940s and early 1950s, sociology proper developed outside
the law faculty. Its development took place partly outside the
University of Oslo — especially through the founding of the in­
dependent interdisciplinary Institute for Social Research in
1950 in Oslo — and partly within the university, through the
establishment of the Institute for Sociology (until 1963 within
the faculty of history and philosophy). Subsequently, the
course in general sociology within the law faculty was trans­
formed into a more specialized course in sociology of law, first
(in the early 1960s) in terms of reading material and finally (in
1968, in the third of three sections of study) in the formal cur­
riculum. But the line of influence from the early development
in the law faculty to the outside developments in general soci­
ology was quite important. Several first generation Norwegian
sociologists had a training in law, and one of the founders of
Norwegian sociology after World War II, the late professor Vil­
helm Aubert, was first associate professor and later full profes­
sor of sociology of law within the law faculty before leaving
that faculty to become professor of general sociology in the so­
cial science faculty in 1971.
    Criminology was the third of the disciplines in question.
Criminology has roots far back into the history of Norwegian
law. The roots may be traced at least to the latter part of the
1800s, and to a fairly strong influence, on Norwegian criminal
law, from positivist criminology and penology taken from conti­
nental Europe. Before World War II, several psychiatrists also
became important contributors. After World War II, the major
first impetus came from penal lawyers within the law faculty,
notably professor emeritus Johs. Andenaes, who at the time
favoured the development of criminology of a sociological
kind. Criminology never became an obligatory subject for law
students (though lectures in criminology have recently been
given within the subject of penal law), but a separate major in

kind in production and trade. This orientation on the part of
the profession probably helped nurture also an interest in the

     Secondly, and partly following from the first point, but also
partly due to a generalized humanistic approach in Norwegian
academia of the 1800s and early 1900s, several important and
influential legal theorists of the 1800s and early 1900s had a
broad social interest and outlook. They programmatically em­
phasized (for example in connection with the far reaching
change to a positivist inspired criminal law around the turn of
the last century) a need for law and legal theory to build on,
and integrate, what was at the time social science.
     But the early story of law and social science would not be
complete without one further remark. There seems to have been
a developmental trend in the relation between law and social
science. Despite the interests and developments sketched
above, legal theorists of later generations, after the broadly ori­
ented « founding fathers » of the 1800s and the early part of the
1900s, have developed a more ambivalent, albeit perhaps un­
easily ambivalent, relationship to the social sciences. On the
face of it, such a development may seem paradoxical. But the
paradox may be resolved. As the social sciences proper devel­
oped on their own grounds, and as social scientists (most no­
tably the economists, but also the political scientists and to
some extent the sociologists) began to take over important posi­
tions and functions in Norwegian society, the need for and im­
petus towards a broad orientation on the part of legal theory be­
came much less pressing. Rather, an urge to renew the profes­
sional base and framework may well have been felt, if not for
the sake of professional survival, at least for the sake of profes­
sional status and prestige, and a narrower, more specialized
technically-legal rule orientation developed. Trends in legal
theory as such, for example so-called Scandinavian legal real­
ism, have certainly been important, but may have found fertile
ground precisely for the sociological reasons discussed here.
Altogether, modem legal science as such has — at least until

610               Developing sociology of law - Norway


very recently — only been very moderately if at all influenced
by social scientific thinking (the exceptions being, i.a., wom­
en’s law, and parts of public law). And in so far as modem le­
gal theorists have been open to an influence, it has to a large
extent been an openness to data and information primarily use­
ful for the legal theorist — a kind of « lawyers’ social science »
— rather than an openness to the social sciences of law devel­
oped on their own grounds.
     This uneasy ambivalence has had at least three conse­
quences. Firstly, it was probably partly responsible (a complex
of other features has obviously also contributed, notably the es­
tablishment of a separate social science faculty) for the exodus
of several social sciences disciplines — economics, political
science and partly sociology — from law. Secondly, and de­
spite programmatic ideals, the ambivalence has implied a cer­
tain incapsulation of legal theory from social science after the
lawyers’ period of greatness as nation builders. Thirdly, it has
produced a certain tension between law proper and those social
science disciplines which have remained in the law faculty,
notably sociology of law and criminology. In fact, until recent­
ly the view that these disciplines most properly belong in the
social science faculty has been maintained by some.
     It would be incorrect, however, not to add that the dis­
tance and tension has had two sides: the sociologists engaged
in sociology of law have been critical and sceptical to the legal
dogmatic approach, wanting, i.a., to develop sociology of law
into an independent discipline basically critical of many of the
functions of law in society. And they have been critical of the
potential use of social science as primarily an additional
method for promoting order and discipline. There has been an
interest in the development of the social sciences of law as
such, as separate subjects. In turn, this has probably increased
the scepticism, and perhaps disappointment, of some lawyers,
also those who initially were instrumental in bringing sociolo­
gists an criminologists in.
